prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling atomic time and frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I still put the optical lattice clock first. It is a single, nameable invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice lets very many neutral atoms be held Doppler- and recoil-free without light shift, and the realization at the 1e-18 level (Ye's strontium clocks and the intercomparisons) has opened measurements that did not exist before: relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, tests of constant variation, dark-matter searches and the coming redefinition of the second. Four colleagues (Lindroth, Pearce, Danielsson, Olsson) ranked it, and Lindroth and I put it first, so the support is real though not broad. The credited pair matches the claim, so the attribution is unusually clean for this field, with two names and no obvious missing third. Many independent laboratories confirm the performance, so it is mature and not a bet on future results.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and breadth. Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already honored combs and ion control, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks a refinement of recognized technology, and only five of eight members ranked it, two of them as low as sixth. The topological-insulator candidate B044 has the widest and deepest support (six members, two first places, four top-three placements) and a theory-plus-experiment story that is easier to explain to non-specialists. My own preference could also reflect a specialist's bias toward measurement science, and the physics payoff (the redefinition of the second, new-physics searches) is still partly prospective.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first, calls it a clearly defined invention distinct from the single-ion clock prizes, and judges the field mature and the recognition timely.
responses.response: I agree on distinctness and maturity, and your point that single-ion clocks were recognized in 2005 and 2012 is the answer I would give to the overlap worry. Where I would go further is on the argument for it as a discovery tool, not just a better clock: the new uncertainty regime is what makes the geodesy and constant-variation tests possible. I also note that you ranked B004 second; I would not trade the clock for it, since the five-name credit there has no clean three-person split.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the quantum spin Hall and Z2 topological insulator work first, as a clean prediction followed by a decisive experimental discovery of a nameable phenomenon, and calls recognition overdue; he ranked lattice clocks only sixth.
responses.response: I accept that B044 is a strong, mature candidate and have kept it as my first alternative. But I disagree that being tied to a nameable phenomenon in nature ranks it above a measurement invention: the clock is an instrument whose capability gain, about two orders of magnitude over the caesium standard, directly produces the new phenomena. I would also press the point that you, Eriksson and Olsson all raise, that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credited names, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves a visible hole in the attribution that the clock pair does not.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators first and lattice clocks only sixth, citing prior prizes on combs and ion traps as a reason for wariness and noting the SI second redefinition has not yet happened.
responses.response: The overlap concern is fair, but I read it differently: Hall and Haensch honored the comb as the frequency ruler, and Wineland the control of single trapped ions. Neither covers neutral-atom lattice trapping at the magic wavelength with many atoms interrogated at once, which is the step that took stability and accuracy to 1e-18. The pending SI redefinition is an administrative timeline, not a scientific uncertainty, because comparisons between independent labs already agree.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and the lattice clock third with the same two names, and values that IceCube needed a genuinely new detector concept and decades of instrumentation.
responses.response: I thank you for ranking the clock third with the same two names, and I share your respect for instrument-driven discovery. On B019 I have a structural difficulty: the supplied credit supports only Halzen, yet IceCube is a very large collaboration where a single-person prize leaves out the people who built the detector, as you acknowledge yourself. The scientific case for neutrino astronomy is strong, but I cannot make the attribution clean with one name, and I would rather see it recognized later with a fuller credit than force it now.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or as incremental.
Whether the broader support for B044 across six members outweighs the narrower but higher first-place support for B024, which is a judgement about the committee's weighting and not a scientific fact.
I rely on memory for details of priority between Katori's proposal and parallel ideas and have not verified them independently.
Whether the redefinition of the second will precede or follow a prize, which affects how the impact is described in the citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for Katori or Ye. I note an indirect field connection: my research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder is documented, and Hall is a laureate whose precision-measurement field is adjacent to the clock work. This is a field and network connection, not a documented personal or institutional tie to the candidates, and I flag it for the chair to judge. My Lund colleagues and my WACQT and Deep Light Vision roles do not relate to the clock candidate.
